mcqs.question: Why is enforcing a layering rule through language-level module visibility generally more reliable than relying on a documented convention?
options: It makes the codebase run faster at runtime
It removes the need for code review entirely
Documented conventions require every engineer to remember and check them manually every time
A forbidden import becomes a compile error, which can't be missed the way a convention can be missed under deadline pressure
mcqs.explanation: Structural enforcement turns a rule violation into something the compiler catches automatically, regardless of reviewer attention or deadline pressure — a documented convention depends entirely on someone remembering and noticing it, which degrades exactly when teams are busiest.

mcqs.question: What does an architecture test / fitness function (like an ArchUnit rule) actually check?
options: It checks that the dependency graph between packages or modules doesn't contain a forbidden edge, failing the build if it does
It measures the runtime performance of each architectural layer
It verifies that unit test coverage meets a minimum percentage per layer
It checks that class names follow the team's naming convention
mcqs.explanation: Architecture tests inspect the actual dependency structure of the code and fail CI when a disallowed import edge exists — they're about structural correctness, not runtime performance, coverage percentages, or naming style.

mcqs.question: How does boundary erosion typically happen in a real codebase over time?
options: A team makes one deliberate, agreed-upon decision to abandon the boundary
A single deadline-driven shortcut goes unnoticed, and later engineers see it already exists and reasonably add more, without any signal that it was a violation
The build tooling silently removes module boundary configuration over time
It only happens when a new framework version changes visibility rules
mcqs.explanation: Erosion is almost always incremental and unintentional — one shortcut becomes precedent for the next engineer, and without an enforcement signal there's nothing distinguishing an approved pattern from an accidental violation until untangling it becomes expensive.

mcqs.question: A team has a wiki page describing their layering rules but no automated check for them. What is the main risk of this approach compared to an enforced boundary?
options: Wiki pages are inherently harder to write than automated tests
A violation is only caught if a reviewer happens to notice it, and the rule doesn't survive team turnover the way an executable check does
Documentation-only rules make the codebase slower to compile
There is no meaningful risk difference between the two approaches
mcqs.explanation: Documentation explains the reasoning but has no enforcement mechanism — a violation slips through unless a reviewer catches it, and new engineers who never read the wiki page have no way to learn the rule exists, unlike a failing CI check.

mcqs.question: A monolith has eroded layering and needs real boundaries introduced. Why does the strangler fig pattern generally beat a full rewrite here?
options: The strangler pattern migrates piece by piece while the system stays fully working at every step, avoiding a long-lived rewrite branch that has to catch up with ongoing changes
The strangler pattern requires no new code to be written
A full rewrite is always technically impossible for a live production system
The strangler pattern automatically detects which boundaries are broken
mcqs.explanation: The strangler pattern's core advantage is incremental, always-working migration — a full rewrite freezes the system in a parallel branch that must chase every change made to the code it's replacing, which is exactly the risk it avoids. It doesn't eliminate the need for new code, and rewrites are possible, just costly.

mcqs.question: A startup applies the full Clean Architecture ring structure to its very first MVP, before any real users exist. What is the main risk being described here?
options: The MVP will be slower to run in production
Clean Architecture cannot be applied to small codebases at all
Real engineering time is spent structuring rules that may not exist yet or may turn out wrong once actual usage reveals the real business logic
The MVP will fail unit tests until all four rings are implemented
mcqs.explanation: The risk is opportunity cost and wasted structure: building elaborate boundaries around business rules that haven't been validated by real usage yet often means the architecture is built around wrong assumptions, and the time spent could have gone toward learning whether the product has customers at all.
